one_liner: SIMD-accelerated Rust priority queue, ~12x faster than std::collections::BinaryHeap on large monotone-key workloads; i32/u32/i64/u64 only.
what_it_does: SimdQuickHeap is a min-priority-queue crate for fixed-width integer keys (i32/u32/i64/u64), pitched as an I/O-efficient alternative to binary/d-ary heaps that keeps its speed once the heap outgrows cache. The Rust API is minimal: SimdQuickHeap::<T>::default(), push, pop -- not a drop-in for BinaryHeap (no iterator, peek, into_sorted_vec, or arbitrary Ord types). An LLM-generated C++ header (cpp/quickheap.hpp) wraps a compiled C ABI in a std::priority_queue-like class (push/pop/try_pop/size/empty), requiring the Rust crate to be built with --features c into a cdylib/staticlib and linked.
how_it_is_fast: Uses QuickSelect-style recursive partitioning of elements into buckets by pivot (median-of-3 by default), keeping only the bottom bucket sorted once it drops below a size threshold (N=16), so most of the heap stays partitioned rather than fully ordered. Partitioning and insertion use SIMD (AVX2, or AVX-512 when compiled in) to compare and move several keys per instruction. This avoids the pointer-chasing and cache misses of array/pointer-based binary heaps once the queue exceeds L2/L3 cache, matching the paper's finding that the gap over BinaryHeap is huge at n=2^25 and nearly gone at n=2^10.
when_to_use: Priority queue over i32/u32/i64/u64 keys, large enough to exceed cache (paper's gains are at n=2^25; negligible at n=2^10)
x86-64 with AVX2 or AVX-512 available at compile time (target-cpu=native / -march=native)
Monotone or near-sorted key sequences (Dijkstra-like, event queues, radix-heap-style workloads) -- where the paper's largest wins are shown
Rust code that can pin to nightly (crate currently requires it) and can vendor a small, very new, unaudited crate
C++ code able to build and statically/dynamically link a Rust cdylib and accept LLM-generated, unreviewed FFI bindings for a throughput win over a naive priority_queue
when_not_to_use: Keys can equal the type's MAX value (e.g. u64::MAX): open issue #6 shows pop() can silently return the wrong element because MAX is used internally as an empty-slot sentinel
Need arbitrary Ord types, custom comparators, decrease-key, iteration, or merge -- only 4 fixed integer types and push/pop are supported
No AVX2/AVX-512 target, or a stable-Rust-only build (crate needs nightly; issue #3 tracks moving off portable-simd)
Heap stays small enough to fit in cache: measured advantage over BinaryHeap collapses to near-parity at n=2^10
Need a mature, widely audited dependency: 35 stars, first public benchmark paper (ESA 2026, arXiv Sept 2026) with no independent replication, and an open correctness bug

integration.dependencies: Rust: ensure_simd 0.1, rand 0.10, wide 1.2. C++ bindings: none beyond the compiled libquickheap.{so,dylib,a} plus quickheap.h/quickheap.hpp.
integration.min_toolchain: Rust nightly (rust-toolchain.toml pins channel = "nightly"); C++17 for the bindings example
integration.platforms: x86-64 only; AVX2 or AVX-512 required at compile time. No other architectures documented.
integration.thread_safety: not documented -- push/pop take &mut self, no Send/Sync mentioned, implying single-threaded/exclusive-access use like std::collections::BinaryHeap
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial -- explain: same push/pop min-heap semantics as BinaryHeap, but restricted to 4 integer key types and missing iterator/peek/into_sorted_vec/generic-Ord support; the C++ wrapper is a separate hand-written class, not a std::priority_queue specialization.

gotchas: Pushing the type's MAX value (e.g. u64::MAX) can corrupt later pop() results -- MAX is used as an internal empty-slot sentinel (issue #6, open, unresolved as of 2026-09-02)
No LICENSE file in the repo (GitHub reports license: null); MIT is declared only via Cargo.toml's license field
Requires nightly Rust today; issue #3 (open) tracks replacing portable-simd with the stable `wide` crate
C++ bindings are explicitly LLM-generated and unreviewed; authors recommend building with panic="abort" so a Rust panic can't unwind across the FFI boundary
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick this over prio_queue (rollbear) or radix-heap when working in Rust against std::collections::BinaryHeap with one of the four supported integer key types and a large, cache-exceeding, monotone-ish workload; it is the only sibling using SIMD partitioning and the only one benchmarked directly against S3Q and monotone radix heaps (1.2-2.8x, more representative than the ~12x BinaryHeap figure). Prefer RadixHeap (radix_heap_rust) instead if you need stable-Rust maturity over a nightly-only crate with an open correctness bug.
verified_claims_summary: On an AMD EPYC 9684X (Zen4), Rust nightly release build (target-cpu=native, fat LTO, single codegen unit), the paper's Table 1 shows SimdQuickHeapAvx2 at 35.6 ns/elem and Avx512 at 32.2 ns/elem versus Rust std::collections::BinaryHeap at 439.6 ns/elem (~12.3x / ~13.7x) on a monotone-key push/pop workload at n=2^25; the gap shrinks to near-parity at n=2^10. No C++ std::priority_queue was benchmarked -- only Rust's BinaryHeap and several C++ competitors (Boost.Heap, S3Q, radix heap, original QuickHeap) via LLM-generated FFI wrappers.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-08-26) but very new (ESA 2026 paper, 35 stars) with an open, unresolved correctness bug on MAX-valued keys; usable as a copyable/vendorable crate, but MIT is only declared in Cargo.toml, not backed by a checked-in LICENSE file.
